subject.title: Self-Portrait with Death Playing the Fiddle
subject.creator: Arnold Böcklin

portrait.credit: Portrait of Arnold Böcklin — Wikimedia Commons

sentences.text: There's a terrifying detail on this violin, and it explains why the painter stopped to listen.
This is Self-Portrait with Death Playing the Fiddle, painted by Arnold Böcklin in 1872.
A bearded painter holds his brush, and behind him a skeleton plays the violin.
According to Alma Mahler, her husband Gustav wrote his Fourth Symphony under the spell of this picture.
A violin should have four strings.
But Böcklin gave Death a fiddle with one.
Death has only one string, yet the painter cannot stop listening.
As if the song ends when that string breaks.
Maybe the last string is his own life.
So is the painter working, or listening to his own end?

meta.title: Death plays for this painter on a single string
meta.description: Self-Portrait with Death Playing the Fiddle was painted by Arnold Böcklin in Munich in 1872. Death stands behind the painter and plays a violin with a single string. Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin.
meta.question: Still working, or listening to his own end?

sources.claim: Self-Portrait with Death Playing the Fiddle is a painted self-portrait executed in 1872 by the Swiss symbolist artist Arnold Böcklin.
Painted in Munich, the painting depicts a bearded Böcklin stalked by a personification of death playing a single-stringed violin in an intimation of his mortality.
According to Alma Mahler, the wife of the composer Gustav Mahler, her husband was "under the spell" of Böcklin's self-portrait when writing the scherzo movement of his Fourth Symphony.
